content: Patients with tuberculosis (TB) who are known to have HIV or live in areas with high HIV prevalence should receive at least six months of treatment with a regimen based on rifampicin or rifabutin. The optimal dosing schedule is daily during both the intensive and continuation phases of treatment. Coexisting conditions such as hepatitis B or C should not prevent the initiation of HIV or TB treatment in people who inject drugs (PWID). Similarly, active drug use, alcohol dependence, or mental health issues should not be used as reasons to withhold treatment. For patients with TB, viral hepatitis, or HIV who also have opioid dependence, opioid agonist therapy should be provided alongside medical treatment. There is no need to delay anti-TB medication, hepatitis treatment, or antiretroviral therapy (ART) until the patient abstains from opioids. The Xpert MTB/RIF test, recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), is a rapid, automated, DNA-based diagnostic tool that can detect TB and rifampicin resistance within two hours. This test is more sensitive than microscopy for detecting TB in people living with HIV and can quickly identify multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), reducing the time to diagnosis and treatment. Integrating TB and HIV services into a comprehensive care package for PWID is essential. TB is the most common AIDS-defining illness in this population, and recognizing TB symptoms is often the first indication of HIV infection. Early and intensified TB case-finding, followed by timely access to TB treatment and ART, reduces mortality and interrupts TB transmission. All PWID living with HIV should be regularly screened for TB using a symptom-based tool that checks for cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Those reporting any of these symptoms should undergo further evaluation for TB and other diseases. Diagnostic workups should follow national guidelines and sound clinical practices to confirm active TB or rule out alternative diagnoses. Regular TB screening is critical, even for individuals receiving isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) or ART. In settings where TB prevalence exceeds 100 cases per 100,000 people, systematic screening for active TB should be considered for high-risk groups, including PWID, regardless of HIV status. Governmental and non-governmental organizations providing services to PWID play a vital role in early TB identification and timely treatment or prevention. WHO strongly recommends using Xpert MTB/RIF as the primary diagnostic test for individuals suspected of having MDR-TB, those living with HIV who exhibit TB symptoms, or those with unknown HIV status but strong clinical evidence of HIV infection. For patients with suspected extrapulmonary TB, diagnostic processes should be expedited using clinical assessments, Xpert MTB/RIF, mycobacterial culture, and chest X-rays. In high HIV-prevalence settings, presumptive anti-TB treatment should be initiated for seriously ill patients when diagnostic tests are negative, and there is no improvement with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Early initiation of TB treatment is crucial to saving lives and preventing further transmission. PWID living with HIV or those newly diagnosed with drug-sensitive TB should receive the standard first-line TB regimen, which includes two months of isoniazid, rifampicin/rifabutin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by four months of rifampicin/rifabutin and isoniazid on a daily schedule. Patients with chronic liver disease should have liver function tested before starting treatment. Those with unstable or advanced liver disease require close monitoring due to the increased risk of hepatotoxicity. PWID with a history of TB treatment interruption or incarceration may be at higher risk for MDR-TB. Patients with both HIV and MDR-TB face complex clinical management challenges, limited treatment options, and poor outcomes. Barriers to TB treatment adherence vary among individuals and settings. Services should consult with PWID to identify effective strategies to overcome these barriers. Evidence shows that adherence improves with directly observed therapy, peer counseling, monetary incentives, and integrated care packages that address psychosocial and healthcare needs. IPT is recommended for people living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB. A six-month course of isoniazid is effective in preventing progression to active TB. In high TB-prevalence settings, continuous IPT for at least 36 months provides additional protection, especially for those on ART. IPT is also effective for PWID, including those co-infected with hepatitis B or C, provided liver function is monitored. Healthcare workers living with HIV should receive ART and IPT if eligible and be offered opportunities to work in low-risk settings. Patients and their families should be educated about TB transmission, infection control, and respiratory hygiene to reduce risks in healthcare and community settings. Preventing the transmission of HIV and viral hepatitis in healthcare and congregate settings is equally important. Standard precautions, such as hand hygiene, safe disposal of sharps, and proper cleaning of equipment, should be implemented to minimize infection risks. Early initiation of ART is recommended for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, as it significantly reduces TB incidence and improves clinical outcomes.
